Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I have lost my connection to my community and culture
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Amara Mensah-Johnson was thirty-two when the August heat trapped her between the chain-link fence of the vacant lot and the rusted side of a delivery truck. The man had smiled, had asked for directions, and then the world had narrowed to the smell of wet cardboard and the brutal, precise weight of his hands. He had pinned her against the damp brick, his breath hot and smelling of mint, while the distant wail of a siren felt like a cruel, indifferent joke. There were moments the details simply vanished, swallowed by the sheer force of his grip, leaving her with a hollowed-out chronology that refused to close. When the memory finally slipped back into her mind, months later, it arrived first as a sharp, familiar ache across her ribs and shoulders, the exact muscles that had torn against his hold. Alongside that physical echo came a hot, sudden fury that made her knuckles whiten around the steering wheel. The trauma did not just break her sleep; it rewired how she saw herself. She found herself staring at the faces of her congregation at Sunday service and wondering why she had been chosen, while others walked home unscathed. The certainty settled deep: she was permanently damaged, fractured in a way that no amount of time could mend, and her mind convinced her that anybody else would have simply walked away. Those beliefs soon dictated her daily routine. Told by her own mind that she was irrevocably altered, Amara began to treat every strong emotion as a threat. On her morning shift at the precinct, when a rookie deputy approached her desk with a heated complaint about a suspect’s alibi, she found herself silently signing off the case file instead of engaging. The fear that the confrontation would unravel her composure sent her retreating into counterfactual scenarios about a life where she had never accepted night patrol. She started declining community dinners and neighborhood watch meetings, quietly severing the very connections that had once grounded her cultural identity. She stopped visiting her mother’s church, where the harmonies once felt like home, and let the distance between her and the diaspora group grow until the group chat went silent. The more she believed she was uniquely broken, the more she avoided situations that might involve disagreement, mistaking silence for safety. Over the next eighteen months, the pattern became a quiet trap. Every time the phantom pain and rage flared during a routine check of her cruiser’s rearview mirror, she doubled down on her withdrawal. She stopped riding solo calls, citing a minor administrative error, but the real reason was the terror that sudden proximity to strangers would spark another wave of physical recall. Her husband, David, noticed the slow retreat first. He saw how she flinched when he raised his voice to call her to dinner, how she would suddenly claim a headache and slip into the bedroom, choosing the hollow comfort of counting backward to avoid the surge of anger or grief. The precinct noticed the shift, too; she was no longer the officer who de-escalated domestic disputes with a steady voice, but the one who paperclipped reports and requested transfers to the archives. She told herself it was merely self-preservation, but the truth was a tightening knot: the memories made her avoid emotional stress, which isolated her further, which convinced her she was permanently damaged, which made the memories feel even more like present threats. When the archives requested a final medical clearance and she found herself unable to breathe in her own cruiser, that was the moment she finally called the clinic. She was not looking for a cure, she admitted quietly, but for a way to stop the memories from dictating her life, and perhaps, just perhaps, to remember who she was before the lot, the truck, and the silence.
